blocks.text: a) Determination of Solubility from Ksp

For this purpose, we need the formula of the compound and Ksp value. Then the unknown molar solubility S is calculated and the concentration of the ions is determined. Table 9.6 shows the relationship between the Ksp values and the solubility of some sparingly soluble compounds.

blocks.caption: Table 9.6 The relation between solubility and solubility products of some salts

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: PbSO₄’s Ksp is printed 1.69 x 10⁻⁴; the text and Table 9.5 give 1.6 × 10⁻⁸, and its solubility gives (1.3 × 10⁻⁴)² = 1.69 × 10⁻⁸. The solubilities are molar (mol dm⁻³), not g dm⁻³: they follow from Ksp, e.g. 1.175 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ for Ca(OH)₂ as in the Sample Problem below.

blocks.title: Sample Problem
blocks.problem: Ca(OH)₂ is a sparingly soluble compound. Its solubility product is 6.5 x 10⁻⁶. Calculate the solubility of Ca(OH)₂.
steps: Let the solubility be represented by S in terms of mol dm⁻³.
The balanced equation is: Ca(OH)₂(aq) ⇌ Ca²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq)
The concentration of OH⁻ is double than the concentration of Ca²⁺, so Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]² = S x (2S)²

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: At equilibrium the concentrations are S and 2S: each Ca(OH)₂ gives one Ca²⁺ and two OH⁻, as the next line uses (2S)².

Hence, at equilibrium stage 1.18 x10⁻² mol dm⁻³ mol dm⁻³ of Ca²⁺ and 2 x 1.18 x10⁻² mol dm⁻³ = 2.36 x 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ OH⁻ are present in the solution. In this way, we have calculated the individual concentrations of Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ ions from the solubility product of Ca(OH)₂.
The presence of a common ion decreases the solubility of a slightly soluble ionic compound. In order to explain it, consider a saturated solution of PbCrO₄, which is a sparingly soluble ionic salt.
Now add Na₂CrO₄ which is a soluble salt. CrO₄²⁻ is the common ion. It combines with Pb²⁺ to form more insoluble PbCrO₄. So equilibrium is shifted to the left to keep Ksp constant.

The solubility product can also help in predicting whether the precipitation of a salt will occur or not. For example, the solubility product of CaSO₄ is 2 x 10⁻⁵. If we add 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ solution Ca²⁺ to 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ solution of SO₄²⁻ ions at 25 °C. The concentrations of each ionic species can be calculated as

blocks.text_alt: [Ca²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = 10⁻²/2 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³; [Ca²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ × 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol² dm⁻⁶ > Ksp of CaSO₄

blocks.text: As the product of concentrations is greater than Ksp, therefore CaSO₄ will precipitate out.

blocks.caption: Ionic product, type of solution and precipitation

blocks.title: Interesting Information!
blocks.text: The shell of this nautilus is composed mainly of calcium carbonate. The nautilus adjusts conditions so shell material is formed when the concentration of calcium ions and carbonate ions in seawater are high enough to precipitate calcium carbonate.
